claim: Hippocampal place cell sequences have been hypothesized to serve diverse purposes including induction of synaptic plasticity, formation and consolidation of long-term memories, and navigation and planning.
source: Hippocampal place cell sequences have been hypothesized to serve as diverse purposes as the induction of synaptic plasticity, formation and consolidation of long-term memories, or navigation and planning.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to existing literature on hippocampal function, though specific citations are not provided in this sentence.

claim: During spatial behaviors of rodents, sequential firing of place cells at the theta timescale (theta sequences) encodes running trajectories.
source: During spatial behaviors of rodents, sequential firing of place cells at the theta timescale (known as theta sequences) encodes running trajectories, which can be considered as one-dimensional behavioral sequences of traversed locations.
evidence: This is a well-established finding in the field, referenced throughout the manuscript.

claim: In a two-dimensional space, each single location can be visited along arbitrary one-dimensional running trajectories.
source: In a two-dimensional space, however, each single location can be visited along arbitrary one-dimensional running trajectories.
evidence: This is a logical observation about spatial navigation in 2D environments.

claim: A place cell will generally take part in multiple different theta sequences in a two-dimensional space.
source: Thus, a place cell will generally take part in multiple different theta sequences, raising questions about how this two-dimensional topology can be reconciled with the idea of hippocampal sequences underlying memory of (one-dimensional) episodes.
evidence: This follows logically from the previous claim about 2D navigation.

claim: The computational model includes cornu ammonis 3 (CA3) and dentate gyrus (DG) regions.
source: Here, we propose a computational model of cornu ammonis 3 (CA3) and dentate gyrus (DG), where sensorimotor input drives the direction-dependent (extrinsic) theta sequences within CA3 reflecting the two-dimensional spatial topology, whereas the intrahippocampal CA3-DG projections concurrently produce intrinsic sequences that are independent of the specific running trajectory.
evidence: This describes the model architecture presented in the manuscript.

claim: Sensorimotor input drives direction-dependent (extrinsic) theta sequences within CA3 reflecting the two-dimensional spatial topology.
source: Here, we propose a computational model of cornu ammonis 3 (CA3) and dentate gyrus (DG), where sensorimotor input drives the direction-dependent (extrinsic) theta sequences within CA3 reflecting the two-dimensional spatial topology, whereas the intrahippocampal CA3-DG projections concurrently produce intrinsic sequences that are independent of the specific running trajectory.
evidence: This is a key prediction of the model presented in the manuscript.

claim: Intrahippocampal CA3-DG projections produce intrinsic sequences that are independent of the specific running trajectory.
source: Here, we propose a computational model of cornu ammonis 3 (CA3) and dentate gyrus (DG), where sensorimotor input drives the direction-dependent (extrinsic) theta sequences within CA3 reflecting the two-dimensional spatial topology, whereas the intrahippocampal CA3-DG projections concurrently produce intrinsic sequences that are independent of the specific running trajectory.
evidence: This is a key prediction of the model presented in the manuscript.

claim: Intrinsic theta sequences are less prominent than extrinsic sequences but can be detected during theta activity.
source: Consistent with experimental data, intrinsic theta sequences are less prominent, but can nevertheless be detected during theta activity, thereby serving as running-direction independent landmark cues.
evidence: This is supported by comparison with experimental data mentioned in the manuscript.

claim: Intrinsic sequences serve as running-direction independent landmark cues.
source: Consistent with experimental data, intrinsic theta sequences are less prominent, but can nevertheless be detected during theta activity, thereby serving as running-direction independent landmark cues.
evidence: This is a functional interpretation proposed by the model.

claim: Intrinsic sequences largely reflect replay and preplay activity during non-theta states.
source: We hypothesize that the intrinsic sequences largely reflect replay and preplay activity during non-theta states.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a hypothesis by the authors.

claim: As a rat navigates in an environment, place cells fire sequentially during one theta cycle (~100 ms).
source: As a rat navigates in an environment, place cells fire sequentially during one theta cycle (∼100 ms) and form time-compressed representations of behavioral experiences (Skaggs et al., 1996), called theta sequences.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Skaggs et al., 1996.

claim: Theta sequences form time-compressed representations of behavioral experiences.
source: As a rat navigates in an environment, place cells fire sequentially during one theta cycle (∼100 ms) and form time-compressed representations of behavioral experiences (Skaggs et al., 1996), called theta sequences.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Skaggs et al., 1996.

claim: Theta sequences were proposed to be driven by extrinsic (extrahippocampal) sensorimotor input.
source: Theta sequences were proposed to be driven by extrinsic (extrahippocampal) sensorimotor input (Foster and Wilson, 2007; Huxter et al., 2008; Romani and Tsodyks, 2015; Yiu et al., 2022), since they are played out in the direction of travel during locomotion and, hence, represent current behavioral trajectories.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Theta sequences are played out in the direction of travel during locomotion.
source: Theta sequences were proposed to be driven by extrinsic (extrahippocampal) sensorimotor input (Foster and Wilson, 2007; Huxter et al., 2008; Romani and Tsodyks, 2015; Yiu et al., 2022), since they are played out in the direction of travel during locomotion and, hence, represent current behavioral trajectories.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations and is a key characteristic of extrinsic sequences.

claim: Non-local activation of place sequences during immobile periods was observed in replay of past locations after the space has been explored.
source: Non-local activation of place sequences during immobile periods was observed in replay of past locations after the space has been explored (Skaggs and McNaughton, 1996; Lee and Wilson, 2002) as well as in preplay (Dragoi and Tonegawa, 2011) of prospective locations before the animal explores a novel environment.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Skaggs and McNaughton, 1996 and Lee and Wilson, 2002.

claim: Preplay of prospective locations occurs before the animal explores a novel environment.
source: Non-local activation of place sequences during immobile periods was observed in replay of past locations after the space has been explored (Skaggs and McNaughton, 1996; Lee and Wilson, 2002) as well as in preplay (Dragoi and Tonegawa, 2011) of prospective locations before the animal explores a novel environment.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dragoi and Tonegawa, 2011.

claim: Some CA3 place cells exhibit out-of-field firing at reward locations.
source: In addition, some CA3 place cells exhibit out-of-field firing at reward locations (Sasaki et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sasaki et al., 2018.

claim: Remote activations of place cells reflect the underlying circuit connectivity rather than the actual location and movement of the animal.
source: These remote activations of place cells reflect the underlying circuit connectivity rather than the actual location and movement of the animal.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the out-of-field firing phenomenon.

claim: A subset of CA3 cell pairs shows rigid theta correlations with peak lags that are independent of the traversal order of their place fields.
source: Furthermore, a subset of CA3 cell pairs shows rigid theta correlations with peak lags that are independent of the traversal order of their place fields (Yiu et al., 2022), suggesting the existence of hard-wired sequences even when sensorimotor drive is present.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yiu et al., 2022.

claim: Rigid theta correlations suggest the existence of hard-wired sequences even when sensorimotor drive is present.
source: Furthermore, a subset of CA3 cell pairs shows rigid theta correlations with peak lags that are independent of the traversal order of their place fields (Yiu et al., 2022), suggesting the existence of hard-wired sequences even when sensorimotor drive is present.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental observation.

claim: Intrinsic sequences driven by intrahippocampal connectivity are less predominantly observed during theta.
source: Such intrinsic sequences that are driven by intrahippocampal connectivity (Tsodyks et al., 1996), although less predominantly observed during theta (Yiu et al., 2022), are generally interpreted as reflecting spatial memories or planning (Kay et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yiu et al., 2022.

claim: Intrinsic sequences are generally interpreted as reflecting spatial memories or planning.
source: Such intrinsic sequences that are driven by intrahippocampal connectivity (Tsodyks et al., 1996), although less predominantly observed during theta (Yiu et al., 2022), are generally interpreted as reflecting spatial memories or planning (Kay et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kay et al., 2020.

claim: Existing models for theta sequences are either fully extrinsic or intrinsic.
source: Existing models for theta sequences are, however, either fully extrinsic or intrinsic.
evidence: This is a characterization of the existing literature.

claim: Extrinsic models often employ short-term plasticity to create synaptic couplings that are temporally stronger along the instantaneous forward direction.
source: The former often employ short-term plasticity (Romani and Tsodyks, 2015; Thurley et al., 2008), which creates synaptic couplings that are temporally stronger along the instantaneous forward direction.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Romani and Tsodyks, 2015 and Thurley et al., 2008.

claim: Intrinsic models use a fixed asymmetrical weight matrix pre-designed to align with one movement trajectory.
source: In contrast, intrinsic models, such as the Tsodyks et al., 1996 model, use a fixed asymmetrical weight matrix pre-designed to align with one movement trajectory (for review see Maurer and McNaughton, 2007; Jaramillo and Kempter, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tsodyks et al., 1996 and review articles.

claim: Neither fully extrinsic nor fully intrinsic models alone can explain the simultaneous presence of rigid and flexible correlations in theta sequences.
source: Neither of these models alone can explain the simultaneous presence of rigid and flexible correlations in theta sequences.
evidence: This is a key motivation for the hybrid model presented in the manuscript.

claim: Lesions of DG abolish non-local activation of CA3 place cells.
source: These intrinsic landmarks need to be stable across time, as shown for some dentate gyrus representations (Hainmueller and Bartos, 2018). We speculate that offline sequences observed during replay and preplay (for review see Buhry et al., 2011; Dragoi and Tonegawa, 2014), would correspond to the intrinsic activity patterns and indicate the context expectation of an animal (which can be detected by a tempotron).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sasaki et al., 2018.

claim: Lesions of DG abolish CA3 theta correlations.
source: Extrinsic sequences are generated in the CA3 layer by short-term synaptic plasticity mechanisms, while the intrinsic sequences are evoked by the CA3-DG feedback loop with fixed asymmetrical weights, as inspired by the experimental evidence that lesions of DG abolish non-local activation of CA3 place cells (Sasaki et al., 2018) and CA3 theta correlations (Ahmadi et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ahmadi et al., 2022.

claim: Extrinsic and intrinsic sequences can propagate simultaneously in separate directions.
source: Extrinsic and intrinsic sequences can propagate simultaneously in separate directions, along the movement trajectory and the pre-designed CA3-DG feedback loops, respectively.
evidence: This is a key prediction of the model presented in the manuscript.

claim: Spike correlations display directionality as the two sequences cross each other at various angles.
source: As a result, spike correlations display directionality as the two sequences cross each other at various angles: The more parallel they are, the stronger the correlation.
evidence: This is a prediction of the model based on the interaction of extrinsic and intrinsic sequences.

claim: The more parallel extrinsic and intrinsic sequences are, the stronger the correlation.
source: As a result, spike correlations display directionality as the two sequences cross each other at various angles: The more parallel they are, the stronger the correlation.
evidence: This is a prediction of the model.

claim: The model simulations are in quantitative agreement with directionality properties found in experimental data.
source: Our simulations are in quantitative agreement with directionality properties found in experimental data (Yiu et al., 2022) and propose that rigid correlation structure can serve as a stable temporal pattern, which is recognizable across multiple movement directions.
evidence: This is supported by comparison with experimental data from Yiu et al., 2022.

claim: Rigid correlation structure can serve as a stable temporal pattern recognizable across multiple movement directions.
source: Our simulations are in quantitative agreement with directionality properties found in experimental data (Yiu et al., 2022) and propose that rigid correlation structure can serve as a stable temporal pattern, which is recognizable across multiple movement directions.
evidence: This is a functional interpretation proposed by the model.

claim: Temporal 'landmark' patterns allow spatial encoding even if sensory-motor experience is lacking.
source: This temporal 'landmark' pattern allows spatial encoding even if sensory-motor experience is lacking and may reflect the mechanistic basis for replay in non-theta states.
evidence: This is a functional interpretation proposed by the model.

claim: Temporal landmark patterns may reflect the mechanistic basis for replay in non-theta states.
source: This temporal 'landmark' pattern allows spatial encoding even if sensory-motor experience is lacking and may reflect the mechanistic basis for replay in non-theta states.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a speculation by the authors.

claim: In the intrinsic Tsodyks et al., 1996 model, phase precession is generated by fixed asymmetrical connectivity between place cells.
source: For intrinsic models, we refer to the Tsodyks et al., 1996 model where phase precession is generated by the fixed asymmetrical connectivity between place cells.
evidence: This is a description of the Tsodyks et al., 1996 model.

claim: In the intrinsic model simulation, all place cells project excitatory synapses to their counterparts with rightward neighboring place fields.
source: In our simulations, all place cells project excitatory synapses to their counterparts with rightward neighboring place fields.
evidence: This describes the specific implementation in the model simulation.

claim: Phase precession in the intrinsic model is determined by how closely the running direction matches the asymmetry direction imposed by the intrinsic connections.
source: Phase precession therefore is determined by how closely the running direction matches the asymmetry direction imposed by the intrinsic connections.
evidence: This is a prediction of the intrinsic model simulation.

claim: The closer the trajectory angle aligns with the asymmetry direction, the more negative is the slope of phase precession in the intrinsic model.
source: The closer the trajectory angle aligns with this asymmetry direction, the more negative is the slope of phase precession (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1E of the manuscript.

claim: In the intrinsic model, the signs of spike correlations between cell pairs remain invariant to the movement direction.
source: Since in this case, the theta sequence only propagates rightwards as place cells are sequentially activated from left to right, the signs of spike correlations between cell pairs remain invariant to the movement direction (Figure 1F, see Methods section: Cross-correlation analysis).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1F and described in the Methods.

claim: Intrinsic models cannot explain experimentally observed directional independence of phase precession and directional dependence of theta spike correlations.
source: Intrinsic models thus cannot explain experimentally observed directional independence of phase precession and directional dependence of theta spike correlations (Huxter et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a limitation of intrinsic models identified by comparison with experimental data.

claim: The extrinsic model is based on a spiking simulation of the originally rate-based model by Romani and Tsodyks, 2015.
source: Our example of an extrinsic model is based on our spiking simulations of the originally rate-based model by Romani and Tsodyks, 2015, where phase precession was explained by symmetric recurrent connections that undergo running direction-dependent attenuation by short-term synaptic depression (STD): place fields with centers behind the current animal position on the trajectory thereby received largely reduced recurrent input resulting in recurrently driven theta sequences to play out only in forward direction (see Methods section: CA3 recurrent connections).
evidence: This describes the basis of the extrinsic model implementation.

claim: In the Romani and Tsodyks, 2015 model, phase precession was explained by symmetric recurrent connections that undergo running direction-dependent attenuation by short-term synaptic depression.
source: Our example of an extrinsic model is based on our spiking simulations of the originally rate-based model by Romani and Tsodyks, 2015, where phase precession was explained by symmetric recurrent connections that undergo running direction-dependent attenuation by short-term synaptic depression (STD): place fields with centers behind the current animal position on the trajectory thereby received largely reduced recurrent input resulting in recurrently driven theta sequences to play out only in forward direction (see Methods section: CA3 recurrent connections).
evidence: This describes the mechanism in the Romani and Tsodyks, 2015 model.

claim: The extrinsic model recovered direction-independent phase precession.
source: We simulated our spiking variant of the Romani and Tsodyks, 2015 model with the same trajectories as the intrinsic model (Figure 1G–I), and recovered direction-independent phase precession (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1H of the manuscript.

claim: In the extrinsic model, theta sequences are played out in the same direction as the movement.
source: Since now, the theta sequences are played out in the same direction as the movement, theta spike correlations are symmetrically reversed (Figure 1I) as shown experimentally in CA1 neurons (Huxter et al., 2008; Yiu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1I and supported by experimental citations.

claim: Theta spike correlations are symmetrically reversed in the extrinsic model, as shown experimentally in CA1 neurons.
source: Since now, the theta sequences are played out in the same direction as the movement, theta spike correlations are symmetrically reversed (Figure 1I) as shown experimentally in CA1 neurons (Huxter et al., 2008; Yiu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1I and supported by citations to Huxter et al., 2008 and Yiu et al., 2022.

claim: In area CA3, theta spike correlations are neither solely extrinsic nor solely intrinsic.
source: In area CA3, however, theta spike correlations are neither solely extrinsic (Yiu et al., 2022; Kay et al., 2020), since phase precession properties change in relation to running directions, nor are they solely intrinsic since reversal of correlation is still observed in most of the sequences (Huxter et al., 2008; Yiu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by multiple experimental citations.

claim: Phase precession properties in CA3 change in relation to running directions.
source: In area CA3, however, theta spike correlations are neither solely extrinsic (Yiu et al., 2022; Kay et al., 2020), since phase precession properties change in relation to running directions, nor are they solely intrinsic since reversal of correlation is still observed in most of the sequences (Huxter et al., 2008; Yiu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by experimental citations.

claim: Reversal of correlation is still observed in most CA3 sequences.
source: In area CA3, however, theta spike correlations are neither solely extrinsic (Yiu et al., 2022; Kay et al., 2020), since phase precession properties change in relation to running directions, nor are they solely intrinsic since reversal of correlation is still observed in most of the sequences (Huxter et al., 2008; Yiu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Huxter et al., 2008 and Yiu et al., 2022.

claim: The model includes both directional and positional modulation of the sensory input to the model place cells.
source: We therefore included both directional and positional modulation of the sensory input to the model place cells (Figure 2A–B) with randomized preferred heading directions (see Methods section: Spatial input).
evidence: This describes a feature of the model implementation shown in Figure 2.

claim: The precession slope observed in the Romani and Tsodyks, 2015 model is limited (-1.13 radians per field size) compared to experimental reports.
source: Furthermore, since the precession slope observed in the Romani and Tsodyks, 2015 model is limited (-1.13 radians per field size, see Figure 1H) as compared to the experimental reports (-4.44 radians (Yiu et al., 2022) and about -2.0 radians (Harris et al., 2002) per field size), we introduced short-term synaptic facilitation (STF) to the sensory input (Berretta and Jones, 1996; Thurley et al., 2008) generating temporally asymmetric depolarization as suggested by intracellular recordings in vivo (Harvey et al., 2009; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1H and compared with experimental data.

claim: Experimental reports show precession slopes of -4.44 radians per field size and about -2.0 radians per field size.
source: Furthermore, since the precession slope observed in the Romani and Tsodyks, 2015 model is limited (-1.13 radians per field size, see Figure 1H) as compared to the experimental reports (-4.44 radians (Yiu et al., 2022) and about -2.0 radians (Harris et al., 2002) per field size), we introduced short-term synaptic facilitation (STF) to the sensory input (Berretta and Jones, 1996; Thurley et al., 2008) generating temporally asymmetric depolarization as suggested by intracellular recordings in vivo (Harvey et al., 2009; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yiu et al., 2022 and Harris et al., 2002.

claim: Short-term synaptic facilitation (STF) was introduced to the sensory input to generate temporally asymmetric depolarization.
source: Furthermore, since the precession slope observed in the Romani and Tsodyks, 2015 model is limited (-1.13 radians per field size, see Figure 1H) as compared to the experimental reports (-4.44 radians (Yiu et al., 2022) and about -2.0 radians (Harris et al., 2002) per field size), we introduced short-term synaptic facilitation (STF) to the sensory input (Berretta and Jones, 1996; Thurley et al., 2008) generating temporally asymmetric depolarization as suggested by intracellular recordings in vivo (Harvey et al., 2009; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a feature of the model implementation supported by citations.

claim: STF amplifies the sensory current at the later part of the field, creating phase precession with steeper slopes and extending the phase range.
source: STF amplifies the sensory current at the later part of the field, thus creating phase precession with steeper slopes thereby extending the phase range (see Methods section: Spatial input).
evidence: This describes the mechanism and effect of STF in the model.

claim: Synaptic weights are stronger between place cells with similar preferred heading directions.
source: Finally, we designated the synaptic weights to be stronger between place cells with similar preferred heading directions (Figure 2C) as has been proposed (Brunel and Trullier, 1998) as a result of Hebbian plasticity applied to directional firing fields.
evidence: This is a feature of the model implementation supported by citation to Brunel and Trullier, 1998.

claim: Stronger synaptic weights between place cells with similar preferred heading directions result from Hebbian plasticity applied to directional firing fields.
source: Finally, we designated the synaptic weights to be stronger between place cells with similar preferred heading directions (Figure 2C) as has been proposed (Brunel and Trullier, 1998) as a result of Hebbian plasticity applied to directional firing fields.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Brunel and Trullier, 1998.

claim: Phase precession has a lower onset and marginal spike phase along best direction than along the worst direction.
source: Phase precession has a lower onset and marginal spike phase along best direction than along the worst (Figure 2G–H), which is consistent with experimental data (Yiu et al., 2022 report mean spike phases ± SEM for best and worst direction of 1.61 ± 0.02 and 2.22 ± 0.03 in radians respectively), reflects that larger depolarizations generally yield shorter latencies.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2G-H and compared with experimental data from Yiu et al., 2022.

claim: Experimental data report mean spike phases ± SEM for best and worst direction of 1.61 ± 0.02 and 2.22 ± 0.03 in radians respectively.
source: Phase precession has a lower onset and marginal spike phase along best direction than along the worst (Figure 2G–H), which is consistent with experimental data (Yiu et al., 2022 report mean spike phases ± SEM for best and worst direction of 1.61 ± 0.02 and 2.22 ± 0.03 in radians respectively), reflects that larger depolarizations generally yield shorter latencies.
evidence: This is cited from Yiu et al., 2022.

claim: Larger depolarizations generally yield shorter latencies.
source: Phase precession has a lower onset and marginal spike phase along best direction than along the worst (Figure 2G–H), which is consistent with experimental data (Yiu et al., 2022 report mean spike phases ± SEM for best and worst direction of 1.61 ± 0.02 and 2.22 ± 0.03 in radians respectively), reflects that larger depolarizations generally yield shorter latencies.
evidence: This is a general principle of neuronal dynamics.

claim: Directionality of the input does not affect spike pair correlations, which remain solely extrinsic.
source: Directionality of the input, although it yields lower spike phases through higher depolarization, does not affect spike pair correlations, which remains solely extrinsic (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Rate directionality and directional bias in recurrent connectivity can render phase precession directionally dependent but are not sufficient to account for intrinsic sequences.
source: Thus, even though rate directionality and directional bias in recurrent connectivity can render phase precession directionally dependent, they are not sufficient to account for intrinsic sequences.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model simulations.

claim: DG is a good candidate region to be involved in phase precession because lesions of it reduce prospective spiking.
source: DG is a good candidate region to be involved in phase precession, since lesions of it were shown to reduce prospective spiking (Sasaki et al., 2018) and to lower the onset phase of phase precession (Ahmadi et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sasaki et al., 2018 and Ahmadi et al., 2022.

claim: Lesions of DG lower the onset phase of phase precession.
source: DG is a good candidate region to be involved in phase precession, since lesions of it were shown to reduce prospective spiking (Sasaki et al., 2018) and to lower the onset phase of phase precession (Ahmadi et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ahmadi et al., 2022.

claim: In the model, neurons in DG receive excitatory synaptic inputs from CA3 place cells.
source: In our model, the neurons in DG receive excitatory synaptic inputs from CA3 place cells (putatively via hilar mossy cells) and project back to the CA3 cells with place field centers at a different location (Equation 3) to induce propagation of intrinsic sequences along a specific spatial direction.
evidence: This describes the model architecture.

claim: DG neurons project back to CA3 cells with place field centers at a different location to induce propagation of intrinsic sequences along a specific spatial direction.
source: In our model, the neurons in DG receive excitatory synaptic inputs from CA3 place cells (putatively via hilar mossy cells) and project back to the CA3 cells with place field centers at a different location (Equation 3) to induce propagation of intrinsic sequences along a specific spatial direction.
evidence: This describes the model mechanism for generating intrinsic sequences.

claim: The connection pattern of DG-CA3 projections could be determined by pre-existing network structure or past experience through associative learning, or both.
source: The connection pattern of DG-CA3 projections (for brevity, we also refer to it as 'DG loop' in the subsequent text) could be determined by pre-existing network structure or past experience through associative learning, or both.
evidence: This is a speculation about the origin of the DG-CA3 connectivity pattern.

claim: When the simulated animal is running in the same direction as the DG-CA3 projection, phase precession starts from a higher phase due to the forward activation of place cells through DG layer.
source: We found that, when the simulated animal is running in the same direction as the DG-CA3 projection, phase precession starts from a higher phase (Figure 3C–D) due to the forward activation of place cells through DG layer (recovering the effect of asymmetric connectivity in the original Tsodyks et al., 1996 model), as compared to the model without DG layer (Figure 2G–H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C-D and compared with Figure 2G-H.

claim: When the animal is running against the DG-CA3 projection, extrinsic sequences are still present in forward direction but intrinsic sequences are played out backward.
source: When, however, the animal is running against the DG-CA3 projection (Figure 3E), extrinsic sequences are still present in forward direction, evoked by the movement of the animal, but the intrinsic sequences are played out backward as determined by the direction of fixed recurrence (see cyan and yellow shaded regions in Figure 3F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3E-F.

claim: Introducing fixed recurrence through DG loops elicits both extrinsic and intrinsic sequences and qualitatively changes theta sequences.
source: Therefore, introducing fixed recurrence through DG loops elicits both extrinsic and intrinsic sequences and qualitatively changes theta sequences.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model simulations.

claim: The model reproduces greater extrinsicity for cell pair activity when running direction aligns with both best place field directions compared to both worst field directions.
source: Our model reproduces a greater extrinsicity for cell pair activity when running direction aligns with both best place field directions as compared to when it aligns to both worst field directions, since along the best direction, cells receive more sensory depolarization, and thus, the movement-dependent extrinsic sequences are more activated.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3J and explained by the model mechanism.

claim: The model explains why pairs with similar preferred heading directions may be less extrinsic than pairs with approximately opposite preferred heading direction.
source: The model also explains, why pairs with similar preferred heading directions may be less extrinsic than pairs with approximately opposite preferred heading direction (dissimilar pairs), since the DG loop preferentially connects CA3 place cells with similar preferred heading directions.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3J and explained by the model mechanism.

claim: Experimental data report ratios of extrinsically to intrinsically correlated CA3 field pairs of 1.57 for both-best directions, 0.41 for both-worst directions, 0.87 for similar pairs and 2.43 for dissimilar pairs.
source: Both of the results follow the same trend as found in experimental data (Yiu et al., 2022 report ratios of extrinsically to intrinsically correlated CA3 field pairs of 1.57 for both-best directions, 0.41 for both-worst directions, 0.87 for similar pairs and 2.43 for dissimilar pairs).
evidence: This is cited from Yiu et al., 2022.

claim: By introducing feedback excitation via the DG layer, intrinsic sequences are able to propagate in fixed directions on top of the movement-dependent extrinsic sequences.
source: Thus, by introducing feedback excitation via the DG layer, intrinsic sequences are able to propagate in fixed directions on top of the movement-dependent extrinsic sequences.
evidence: This is a summary of the model mechanism.

claim: Theta sequence directionality is reflected through the change in spike correlation, which varies as a function of the difference between the direction of DG feedback and movement direction.
source: Theta sequence directionality is reflected through the change in spike correlation, which varies as a function of the difference between the direction of DG feedback and movement direction.
evidence: This is a prediction of the model.

claim: The combination of extrinsic and intrinsic theta sequence activity is robust regarding changes of the parameters of short-term synaptic plasticity.
source: The combination of extrinsic and intrinsic theta sequence activity is robust regarding changes of the parameters of short-term synaptic plasticity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), as well as running speed (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), as long as place fields are wide enough to allow spikes in sufficiently many theta cycles.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The combination of extrinsic and intrinsic theta sequence activity is robust regarding changes in running speed, as long as place fields are wide enough to allow spikes in sufficiently many theta cycles.
source: The combination of extrinsic and intrinsic theta sequence activity is robust regarding changes of the parameters of short-term synaptic plasticity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), as well as running speed (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), as long as place fields are wide enough to allow spikes in sufficiently many theta cycles.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: One prediction of the DG-loop model is that DG would contribute to the temporal organization of spike sequences in CA3.
source: One prediction of the DG-loop model, consistent with findings from DG lesion experiments (Ahmadi et al., 2022), is that DG would contribute to the temporal organization of spike sequences in CA3.
evidence: This is a prediction of the model consistent with experimental findings.

claim: A DG lesion reduces theta compression in sequence activity.
source: We found that a DG lesion would reduce theta compression in sequence activity.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: The DG lesion reduces the spike phase and phase range of phase precession.
source: The DG lesion also reduces the spike phase and phase range of phase precession (Figure 4D), which indicates the participation of DG loops in high-phase spiking.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Weaker phase precession and theta compression stress the important role of DG in temporal organization of CA3 sequences.
source: Both weaker phase precession and theta compression stress the important role of DG in temporal organization of CA3 sequences.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lesion simulation results.

claim: Intrinsic sequences with a higher marginal spike phase can be seen along the belt of DG-loop projections and are extended to the outside of trajectory predicting 'off-track' spikes at high phases.
source: We further resolve the precession slope, onset and marginal phase for each place cell into 2-d maps (Figure 5B and D). Intrinsic sequences with a higher marginal spike phase can be clearly seen along the belt of DG-loop projections and are even extended to the outside of trajectory predicting 'off-track' spikes at high phases.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B and D.

claim: Extrinsic sequences represent trajectory direction while intrinsic sequences represent associative memory towards specific locations.
source: The results demonstrate the distinct roles of extrinsic and intrinsic sequences in 2-d spatial encoding. The former represents trajectory direction while the latter the associative memory towards specific locations.
evidence: This is a functional interpretation of the model results.

claim: Extrinsic and intrinsic sequences can be played out at the same time separately in different directions and only interact with each other when they overlap.
source: They can be played out at the same time separately in different directions and only interact with each other when they overlap.
evidence: This is a prediction of the model.

claim: The interaction between extrinsic and intrinsic sequences is reflected in directional dependence of phase precession properties, most notably the higher spike phases from the DG-CA3 recurrent input.
source: The interaction is reflected in directional dependence of phase precession properties, most notably the higher spike phases from the DG-CA3 recurrent input, as well as increased intrinsicity of pair correlation and extended firing fields along the orientation of the DG-loop projections.
evidence: This is a prediction of the model shown in the figures.

claim: Intrinsic sequences triggered out-of-field firing at late theta phases.
source: Intrinsic sequences also triggered out-of-field firing (Figure 5B, D and G) at late theta phases.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B, D and G.

claim: Feng et al., 2015 find that theta sequences on a first exposure of a novel linear track are much weaker.
source: Although Feng et al., 2015 find that theta sequences on a first exposure of a novel linear track are indeed much weaker (maybe only reflecting intrinsic sequences), their results nevertheless indicate a very fast learning time scale that is hard to reconcile with recurrent learning of a full spatial topology (particularly the generalization to 2-d).
evidence: This is cited from Feng et al., 2015.

claim: Extrinsic sequences can be generated by spatial input alone relying only on the short-term facilitation mechanism.
source: Our simulations show that extrinsic sequences can still be generated by spatial input alone (Figure 6A), relying only on the short-term facilitation mechanism.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Simulating CA3 activity with lesioned DG abolishes the temporal organization of theta sequence and reduces the phase range even without CA3 recurrence.
source: Simulating CA3 activity with lesioned DG similarly abolishes the temporal organization of theta sequence and reduces the phase range (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The temporal order of extrinsic sequences could be coordinated solely by sensorimotor drive and does not necessarily require CA3 recurrence.
source: The results demonstrate that the temporal order of extrinsic sequences could be coordinated solely by sensorimotor drive and does not necessarily require CA3 recurrence.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulations without CA3 recurrence.

claim: Intrinsic activity may serve a role to identify certain location-direction pairs independent of the current trajectory.
source: Simulations of trajectories in 2-d (Figure 5) suggest intrinsic activity may serve a role to identify certain location-direction pairs independent of the current trajectory.
evidence: This is a functional interpretation based on the 2-d simulations.

claim: The intrinsic sequences signal a stable 'landmark' (location/direction pair) cue by a temporal code that is invariant to different directions of approach.
source: Here, we follow this idea by evaluating the hypothesis that the intrinsic sequences signal a stable 'landmark' (location/direction pair) cue by a temporal code that is invariant to different directions of approach.
evidence: This is the hypothesis being tested with the tempotron analysis.

claim: The tempotron trained on the intrinsic sequence from the DG loop is able to recognize the sequence patterns produced for all running directions.
source: We found that the tempotron trained on the intrinsic sequence from the DG loop is able to recognize the sequence patterns produced for all running directions, while the tempotron trained without a DG-loop fails to identify the extrinsic sequences most of the time (see accuracies in Figure 7D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The tempotron trained without a DG-loop fails to identify the extrinsic sequences most of the time.
source: We found that the tempotron trained on the intrinsic sequence from the DG loop is able to recognize the sequence patterns produced for all running directions, while the tempotron trained without a DG-loop fails to identify the extrinsic sequences most of the time (see accuracies in Figure 7D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Spike patterns induced by intrinsic sequences remain similar to the training pattern despite being approached in other directions.
source: The reason is that the spike patterns induced by intrinsic sequences remain similar to the training pattern despite being approached in other directions (see sequential contributions in Figure 7E), while spike patterns for the no-loop condition are different between training and testing (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7E and F.

claim: Sequences always contain components that propagate along the projection direction of DG loop.
source: Sequences always contain components that propagate along the projection direction of DG loop, while, without such a loop, they only propagate along the running direction.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8.

claim: Without a DG loop, sequences only propagate along the running direction.
source: Sequences always contain components that propagate along the projection direction of DG loop, while, without such a loop, they only propagate along the running direction.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8.

claim: Intrinsic sequences can provide a stable correlation signal which allows reliable decoding of locations through temporal correlations.
source: Our results show that intrinsic sequences can provide a stable correlation signal which allows reliable decoding of locations through temporal correlations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the tempotron analysis.

claim: The intrinsic temporal code remains detectable even when mixed with extrinsic sequences.
source: The intrinsic temporal code remains detectable even when mixed with extrinsic sequences.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the tempotron analysis.

claim: Both extrinsic and intrinsic mechanisms are required to explain experimental reports that phase precession and spike timing correlations are non-homogeneous across running directions.
source: We presented a model of hippocampal theta sequences in 2-d environments, suggesting that both extrinsic and intrinsic mechanisms are required to explain experimental reports that phase precession and spike timing correlations are non-homogeneous across running directions.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the manuscript.

claim: Phase precession becomes directional by including direction-dependent sensory input into a purely extrinsic model.
source: Although phase precession already becomes directional by including direction-dependent sensory input into a purely extrinsic model, directionality of spike timing correlations cannot be explained by such a model.
evidence: This is shown in the model simulations.

claim: Directionality of spike timing correlations cannot be explained by a purely extrinsic model with direction-dependent sensory input.
source: Although phase precession already becomes directional by including direction-dependent sensory input into a purely extrinsic model, directionality of spike timing correlations cannot be explained by such a model.
evidence: This is shown in the model simulations.

claim: The correlation preference could be implemented by fixed recurrent loops via a model DG layer.
source: We, however, demonstrated that the correlation preference could be implemented by fixed recurrent loops via a model DG layer.
evidence: This is demonstrated in the model simulations.

claim: DG lesions plus compensatory sensory drive can abolish the theta compression effect in CA3 spiking activity.
source: We further supported the model assumptions by showing that DG lesions plus compensatory sensory drive can abolish the theta compression effect in CA3 spiking activity (Ahmadi et al., 2022).
evidence: This is shown in the model simulations and compared with experimental findings from Ahmadi et al., 2022.

claim: Intrinsic sequences could function as stable signatures that act as anchors of the spatial code.
source: By employing a spike-based temporal pattern decoder (tempotron), we showed that the intrinsic sequences could function as stable signatures that act as anchors of the spatial code.
evidence: This is shown in the tempotron analysis.

claim: Early intrinsic models were challenged owing to their inability to generate phase precession in backward travel.
source: Early intrinsic models (Tsodyks et al., 1996) were challenged owing to their inability to generate phase precession in backward travel (Figure 1E, also see Cei et al., 2014), as well as the predominantly extrinsic correlations observed in CA1 (Huxter et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a known limitation of intrinsic models cited from the literature.

claim: Extrinsic sequences dominate over intrinsic sequences as indicated by the majority of field pairs being extrinsic.
source: Also, extrinsic sequences still dominate over intrinsic sequences as indicated by the majority of field pairs being extrinsic (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3J.

claim: The reduced expression of phase precession in reverse runs and the dominance of extrinsic sequences are in accordance with experimental data.
source: Both the reduced expression of phase precession in reverse runs and the dominance of extrinsic sequences are in accordance with the experimental data (Yiu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yiu et al., 2022.

claim: The mixture of extrinsic and intrinsic mechanisms naturally gives rise to the directionality of spike correlations and phase distributions.
source: The mixture of extrinsic and intrinsic mechanisms in our theory, naturally gives rise to the directionality of spike correlations and phase distributions.
evidence: This is a key result of the model.

claim: As the trajectory aligns itself with the DG loops, the ratio of intrinsic to extrinsic sequences increases.
source: As the trajectory aligns itself with the DG loops, the ratio of intrinsic to extrinsic sequences increases.
evidence: This is a prediction of the model.

claim: Spike correlations become more rigid and the phase distribution is shifted upward due to the accumulated synaptic transmission delay from the reverberating activity between CA3 and DG populations.
source: As a result, spike correlations become more rigid and the phase distribution is shifted upward due to the accumulated synaptic transmission delay from the reverberating activity between CA3 and DG populations.
evidence: This is a prediction of the model mechanism.

claim: Adding directional sensory input activates extrinsic sequences in the best direction more strongly, leading to an association between best-angle (worst-angle) pairs and extrinsicity (intrinsicity).
source: Adding directional sensory input activates extrinsic sequences in the best direction more strongly, and hence, leads to an association between best-angle (worst-angle) pairs and extrinsicity (intrinsicity).
evidence: This is a prediction of the model mechanism.

claim: The model predictions are corroborated by past reports of higher spike phases in the non-preferred arm of a T-maze.
source: These predictions of our model are corroborated by past reports of higher spike phases in the non-preferred arm of a T-maze (Kay et al., 2020) as well as the association of rigid correlations with upward shifts in spike phases and an increase in worst-angle pairs (Yiu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kay et al., 2020.

claim: The model predictions are corroborated by the association of rigid correlations with upward shifts in spike phases and an increase in worst-angle pairs.
source: These predictions of our model are corroborated by past reports of higher spike phases in the non-preferred arm of a T-maze (Kay et al., 2020) as well as the association of rigid correlations with upward shifts in spike phases and an increase in worst-angle pairs (Yiu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yiu et al., 2022.

claim: The model predicts direction-dependent expansion of place fields, or even multiple place fields, with the intrinsic sequence's target location exhibiting late spike phases and higher phase precession onsets.
source: Since intrinsic sequences can also propagate outside the trajectory (out-of-field firing in Figure 5) and activate place cells non-locally, our model predicts direction-dependent expansion of place fields, or even multiple place fields, with the intrinsic sequence's target location exhibiting late spike phases and higher phase precession onsets.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the model simulations shown in Figure 5.

claim: Remote activation during locomotion has been observed where CA3 place cells preferentially firing at one arm of the maze were also activated at reward locations at other arms.
source: Remote activation during locomotion has already been observed in a previous study (Sasaki et al., 2018) where CA3 place cells preferentially firing at one arm of the maze were also activated at reward locations at other arms.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sasaki et al., 2018.

claim: Skewness of place fields has been reported showing place fields to be asymmetrically expanded opposite to the direction of travel.
source: Skewness of place fields has been reported by a number of studies (Mehta et al., 1997; Shen et al., 1997; Mehta et al., 2000; Ekstrom et al., 2001; Lee et al., 2004; Burke et al., 2008; Cei et al., 2014; Roth et al., 2012; Dong et al., 2021) showing place fields to be asymmetrically expanded opposite to the direction of travel.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Place field skewness was connected to plasticity as it develops after repeated traversal and due to its dependence on NMDA receptor activation.
source: This effect was connected to plasticity as it develops after repeated traversal, and due to its dependence on NMDA receptor activation (Ekstrom et al., 2001; Burke et al., 2008; Shen et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ekstrom et al., 2001, Burke et al., 2008, and Shen et al., 1997.

claim: Place fields in CA3 were more skewed than in CA1.
source: Yet some prior studies (Lee et al., 2004; Roth et al., 2012) did show that place fields in CA3 were more skewed than in CA1, which our model would explain by CA3 expressing more intrinsic sequences than CA1 consistent with prior experimental observations (Yiu et al., 2022 reported ratios of extrinsically to intrinsically driven cell pairs of 1.44 in CA1 and 1.23 in CA3).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2004 and Roth et al., 2012.

claim: CA3 expresses more intrinsic sequences than CA1.
source: Yet some prior studies (Lee et al., 2004; Roth et al., 2012) did show that place fields in CA3 were more skewed than in CA1, which our model would explain by CA3 expressing more intrinsic sequences than CA1 consistent with prior experimental observations (Yiu et al., 2022 reported ratios of extrinsically to intrinsically driven cell pairs of 1.44 in CA1 and 1.23 in CA3).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yiu et al., 2022.

claim: A further prediction of hard-wired DG loops is that the resulting activity patterns (intrinsic sequences) should not remap under conditions of global or partial remapping.
source: A further prediction of hard-wired DG loops is that the resulting activity patterns (intrinsic sequences) should not remap under conditions of global or partial remapping (Leutgeb et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a prediction of the model with reference to remapping literature.

claim: The same intrinsic sequence components should be observable in multiple environments.
source: Instead the same intrinsic sequence components should be observable in multiple environments, however, they might only be seen in a small fraction and thus this prediction is potentially hard to test.
evidence: This is a prediction of the model.

claim: The back-projection from CA3 to DG is a crucial anatomical prerequisite of the model.
source: The back-projection from CA3 to DG is a crucial anatomical prerequisite of our model, but was rarely explored compared to the feed-forward inputs via the perforant pathway.
evidence: This is a statement about the anatomical basis of the model.

claim: Pyramidal cells in CA3 innervate the mossy cells at the DG hilus.
source: Pyramidal cells in CA3 innervate the mossy cells at the DG hilus (Scharfman, 1994; Scharfman, 2016), which then project to granule cells through both excitatory and inhibitory pathways (Hsu et al., 2016; Scharfman, 1995; Larimer and Strowbridge, 2008; Soriano and Frotscher, 1994), and subsequently back to CA3 pyramidal cells.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Scharfman, 1994 and Scharfman, 2016.

claim: Mossy cells project to granule cells through both excitatory and inhibitory pathways.
source: Pyramidal cells in CA3 innervate the mossy cells at the DG hilus (Scharfman, 1994; Scharfman, 2016), which then project to granule cells through both excitatory and inhibitory pathways (Hsu et al., 2016; Scharfman, 1995; Larimer and Strowbridge, 2008; Soriano and Frotscher, 1994), and subsequently back to CA3 pyramidal cells.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: An optogenetic study showed that the net effect of mossy cells on granule cells was predominantly inhibitory.
source: An optogenetic study (Hsu et al., 2016) showed that the net effect of mossy cells on granule cells was predominantly inhibitory, suggesting that the DG ensembles excited by mossy cell synaptic drive are sparsified by suppressing unwanted out-of-ensemble activity.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hsu et al., 2016.

claim: Reliable excitatory effect could be observed when granule cells were depolarized.
source: Indeed, past studies showed that reliable excitatory effect could be observed when granule cells were depolarized (Scharfman, 1995) and when they received back-propagation of sharp wave bursts from CA3 population (Penttonen et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Scharfman, 1995.

claim: Reliable excitatory effect could be observed when granule cells received back-propagation of sharp wave bursts from CA3 population.
source: Indeed, past studies showed that reliable excitatory effect could be observed when granule cells were depolarized (Scharfman, 1995) and when they received back-propagation of sharp wave bursts from CA3 population (Penttonen et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Penttonen et al., 1998.

claim: The excitatory recurrent pathway from CA3 via DG exists and might allow activity reverberation between two layers.
source: This indicates that the excitatory recurrent pathway from CA3 via DG exists and might allow activity reverberation between two layers.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited studies.

claim: The model assumes a connectivity pattern in the DG loops in which neurons activate the neighbours along a specific direction, as inspired by Hebb's phase sequences.
source: Our model assumed a connectivity pattern in the DG loops, in which neurons activate the neighbours along a specific direction, as inspired by Hebb's phase sequences (Hebb, 1949) and, hence, replay of the loop would activate a spatially plausible virtual trajectory.
evidence: This is inspired by Hebb's phase sequences cited from Hebb, 1949.

claim: The loop connectivity could either arise from previous learning, or might be present already beforehand.
source: The loop connectivity could either arise from previous learning, or might be present already beforehand (Dragoi and Tonegawa, 2013), with spatial topology inherited by associating 2-d sensory features to cell ensembles in the loop (Leibold, 2020).
evidence: This is a speculation about the origin of the loop connectivity with citations.

claim: The model includes heading direction as part of the sensory input, as inspired by past literature showing CA1, CA3, and DG place cells exhibit directional selectivity in firing rates.
source: Different from other phase precession models, we also included heading direction as part of the sensory input, as inspired by past literature that CA1 (Markus et al., 1995; Acharya et al., 2016; Stefanini et al., 2020), CA3 (Mankin et al., 2019), and DG place cells (Stefanini et al., 2020) exhibit directional selectivity in firing rates, potentially inherited from the upstream head-direction cells in the medial entorhinal cortex (Giocomo et al., 2014) and postsubiculum (Taube et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The directional drive immediately translates to phase directionality in theta sequences.
source: As a result, the directional drive immediately translates to phase directionality in theta sequences, partly contributing to the upward shift of the phase distribution in the worst angles.
evidence: This is a prediction of the model mechanism.

claim: Phase directionality arises naturally from the intracellular dynamics of a spike-based model, where stronger depolarization causes earlier spiking.
source: Such phase directionality arises naturally from the intracellular dynamics of a spike-based model, where stronger depolarization causes earlier spiking.
evidence: This is a general principle of neuronal dynamics.

claim: Phase-rate dependence has been used in previous models where the increasing depolarization within place fields directly relates to decreasing spike phases.
source: This phase-rate dependence has already been used in previous models (Harris et al., 2002; Mehta et al., 2002; Thurley et al., 2008), where the increasing depolarization within place fields directly relates to decreasing spike phases.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous models.

claim: The causal effect of firing rate on spike phases was disputed by Huxter et al., 2003 as they showed that precession slopes and spike phases remained the same between high- and low-spiking runs.
source: The causal effect of firing rate on spike phases, however, was disputed by Huxter et al., 2003 as they showed that precession slopes and spike phases remained the same between high- and low-spiking runs, suggesting that the phase is not single-handedly determined by firing rate.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Huxter et al., 2003.

claim: In the model, firing rate is determined by both low-phase spiking from sensory input and high-phase spike arrivals of DG-CA3 loops.
source: In our model, firing rate is determined by both low-phase spiking from sensory input and high-phase spike arrivals of DG-CA3 loops, both producing opposing effects on the phase distribution.
evidence: This describes the model mechanism.

claim: Spike phases are not fully determined by firing rate depending on the strength and geometry of the DG-CA3 connectivity.
source: Thus, depending on the strength and geometry of the DG-CA3 connectivity, spike phases are not fully determined by firing rate.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the model mechanism.

claim: The spike patterns of intrinsic sequences can serve as a stable landmark which remains decodable across multiple running directions.
source: By using a tempotron to decode the spike patterns, we show that the spike patterns of intrinsic sequences can serve as a stable landmark which remains decodable across multiple running directions.
evidence: This is shown in the tempotron analysis.

claim: The invariant temporal patterns could serve as anchors of spatial memories in a novel environment, since place fields only stabilize after the animal becomes familiar with the environment.
source: The invariant temporal patterns could serve as anchors of spatial memories in a novel environment, since place fields only stabilize after the animal becomes familiar with the environment (Wilson and McNaughton, 1993).
evidence: This is a functional interpretation with citation to Wilson and McNaughton, 1993.

claim: Pre-existing sequence motifs can encode position based on their temporal relations alone even when spikes are not spatially tuned to a location.
source: The pre-existing sequence motifs, even at times when the spikes of the neurons are not spatially tuned to a location, can still encode the position based on their temporal relations alone.
evidence: This is a functional interpretation of the model.

claim: The idea that pre-existing sequence motifs can encode position has previously been spelled out and numerically verified.
source: The idea has previously been spelled out (Cheng, 2013) and numerically verified (Leibold, 2020; Parra-Barrero and Cheng, 2023) with multiple fixed sequences that form a decodable spatial representation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cheng, 2013, Leibold, 2020, and Parra-Barrero and Cheng, 2023.

claim: Intrinsic sequences may act as a scaffold around which a new spatial code can be built for new but similar behavioral contexts.
source: Intrinsic sequences may thus act as a scaffold around which a new spatial code can be built for new but similar behavioral contexts, where similarity could for example be identified by a salient feature.
evidence: This is a functional interpretation and speculation.

claim: Once the behavioral context of a situation changes, new intrinsic sequences would be observable.
source: Once the behavioral context of a situation changes, new intrinsic sequences would be observable.
evidence: This is a prediction of the model.

claim: Intrinsic landmarks need to be stable across time, as shown for some dentate gyrus representations.
source: These intrinsic landmarks need to be stable across time, as shown for some dentate gyrus representations (Hainmueller and Bartos, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hainmueller and Bartos, 2018.

claim: Offline sequences observed during replay and preplay would correspond to the intrinsic activity patterns and indicate the context expectation of an animal.
source: We speculate that offline sequences observed during replay and preplay (for review see Buhry et al., 2011; Dragoi and Tonegawa, 2014), would correspond to the intrinsic activity patterns and indicate the context expectation of an animal (which can be detected by a tempotron).
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a speculation with citations to review articles.

claim: The functional roles of intrinsic sequences may not be limited to spatial memories.
source: The functional roles of intrinsic sequences may thus not be limited to spatial memories.
evidence: This is a speculation about broader functional roles.

claim: In the spatial domain, intrinsic sequences could be interpreted as spatial trajectories.
source: While, in the spatial domain, intrinsic sequences could be interpreted as spatial trajectories (Kay et al., 2020; Sasaki et al., 2018), virtual non-spatial trajectories could represent working memories contents (Jensen et al., 1996) available for general decision making processes.
evidence: This is a functional interpretation with citations.

claim: Virtual non-spatial trajectories could represent working memories contents available for general decision making processes.
source: While, in the spatial domain, intrinsic sequences could be interpreted as spatial trajectories (Kay et al., 2020; Sasaki et al., 2018), virtual non-spatial trajectories could represent working memories contents (Jensen et al., 1996) available for general decision making processes.
evidence: This is a speculation with citation to Jensen et al., 1996.
